data.title: Kernel ridge (RBF) on log-temperatures with standard scaling
data.hypothesis: The map from sensor time-series to conductivities is smooth but nonlinear (diffusion timescales scale ~1/k, so temperature decay is roughly exponential in k*t). Log features linearise exponential decay, and an RBF kernel ridge with tuned alpha/bandwidth is a strong, well-regularised smooth interpolant for n=3000 (cheap O(n^2)).

data.hypothesis: If log-temperature is near-linear in conductivity (or log k), a heavily-tuned ridge gives a fast, low-variance baseline and tells us how much nonlinearity remains; correlated time samples are handled by L2 shrinkage.

data.title: PCA-denoised kernel ridge
data.hypothesis: The 80 features are highly correlated smooth time traces corrupted by noise; projecting onto ~20 principal components removes noise directions before the RBF kernel, improving the distance metric and reducing variance.

data.title: Distance-weighted kNN on PCA-reduced features
data.hypothesis: Instance-based check of local smoothness of the inverse map; with 3000 simulations covering a 4-D parameter space and PCA denoising, kNN gives a nonparametric reference that is robust to nonlinearity and informs kernel bandwidth choice.

summary: Extra-trees on log-temperature features with PCA denoising

data.title: Extra-trees on log-temperature features with PCA denoising
data.hypothesis: Conductivity controls diffusion time-scales, so temperature decay is roughly exponential in k; log features linearise this relationship. PCA to ~20 components averages out sensor noise across the 80 correlated time samples, and extra-trees' random splits give low-variance smooth approximations of the mildly nonlinear inverse map with almost no tuning cost.

data.title: Histogram GBM per conductivity on PCA-compressed raw signals
data.hypothesis: Each segment conductivity depends mostly on a few informative latent directions (local decay rates near the corresponding sensor). Boosting with small learning rate and moderate leaves captures the monotone nonlinear k-vs-decay relationship and interactions between neighbouring segments better than bagging, while L2 regularisation guards against noise.

data.hypothesis: Keeping all 80 log-features lets trees pick specific sensor/time pairs most sensitive to each segment's k (e.g. early-time response near interfaces) that PCA could mix away; subsampling features at 0.3 decorrelates trees and averages noise.

author: ideator-ensembles
summary: Ridge-residual boosting: linear base + extra-trees on residuals

data.title: Ridge-residual boosting: linear base + extra-trees on residuals
data.hypothesis: The inverse map is likely near-linear in log-features (smooth dependence of decay rates on k) plus a nonlinear correction. Trees alone approximate the linear trend with piecewise-constant staircases, wasting capacity and causing extrapolation error; fitting ridge first and an extra-trees ensemble on its residuals combines linear extrapolation with nonlinear correction, which should push rel_l2 toward the 0.05 target.

summary: Torch MLP with moderate width, GELU, weight decay and light dropout on standardized raw features

data.title: Torch MLP with moderate width, GELU, weight decay and light dropout on standardized raw features
data.hypothesis: The map from 80 sensor-time temperatures to 4 conductivities is smooth but nonlinear (temperatures depend on k through diffusion time scales, roughly like exp(-k t)). A LayerNorm/GELU MLP trained with AdamW and cosine LR should capture this nonlinearity much better than linear models. With 3000 samples, a 512x256x128 network plus light dropout and weight decay gives enough capacity while limiting overfitting to sensor noise.

author: ideator-neural
summary: Torch MLP on PCA-denoised log features with tanh activation

data.title: Torch MLP on PCA-denoised log features with tanh activation
data.hypothesis: Heat-equation solutions decay roughly exponentially in time at a rate tied to k, so log temperatures make the dependence on k closer to linear. The 80 features are highly correlated across time, so PCA to about 24 components keeps the dominant diffusion modes and removes independent sensor noise. A smooth tanh MLP fits the remaining low-dimensional smooth map well, and the noise filtering should improve generalization.

author: ideator-neural
summary: sklearn MLP with stronger L2 on sqrt features (cheap regularisation contrast)

data.title: sklearn MLP with stronger L2 on sqrt features (cheap regularisation contrast)
data.hypothesis: This checks whether stronger L2 weight penalty beats dropout and weight decay for this noisy inverse problem. Noise amplification is the main risk in ill-posed inverse maps, and a larger alpha smooths the learned inverse. The sqrt transform compresses the dynamic range like log does, without blowing up near-zero temperatures. Early stopping caps compute.

author: ideator-neural
summary: Custom deep-ensemble of residual MLPs with Gaussian input-noise augmentation

data.title: Custom deep-ensemble of residual MLPs with Gaussian input-noise augmentation
data.hypothesis: Test inputs carry measurement noise, so injecting Gaussian noise into the standardized inputs during training acts like Tikhonov regularization matched to the inverse problem. A residual MLP with SiLU and LayerNorm trains stably. Averaging 3 seeds cuts variance, which should help push rel_l2 below 0.05. The ensemble is kept small to fit the CPU budget.

data.title: Log-temperature kernel ridge (decay-rate linearisation)
data.hypothesis: In a Dirichlet heat problem each sensor signal decays roughly as a sum of exponentials exp(-lambda_n t), and the eigenvalues lambda_n scale with the conductivities. Taking logs turns these decays into near-linear functions of time whose slopes encode k, so the inverse map becomes smoother and close to linear. An RBF kernel ridge model can then capture the remaining mild nonlinearity, such as the interface coupling between segments, using only 3000 samples. It is also cheap at O(n^2) with n=3000.

author: ideator-domain
summary: Ridge on log features (cheap linear-in-log-decay probe)

data.title: Ridge on log features (cheap linear-in-log-decay probe)
data.hypothesis: If log-temperature slopes are close to linear in k, a regularised linear model on log features should already beat the 0.33 baseline by a wide margin. It also tells us how much of the remaining error is nonlinearity rather than noise. It costs almost no compute and lets later budget go to nonlinear learners only if needed.

author: ideator-domain
summary: Physics-derived features (decay rates, time derivatives, inter-sensor gradients) + RBF KRR

data.title: Physics-derived features (decay rates, time derivatives, inter-sensor gradients) + RBF KRR
data.hypothesis: The conductivity in each segment controls two things: the local decay rate (d log u/dt) and the flux between neighbouring sensors (spatial differences of u). The model fits per-sensor log-decay slopes, both global and late-time (where the dominant eigenmode isolates the slowest effective conductance). It adds time finite differences of log u, which act as a proxy for u_t/u and so for the local Laplacian scaled by k, and adjacent-sensor log differences, which proxy the gradient and flux. These are physically aligned summaries and should sharpen the RBF metric. Both possible 4x20 layouts (sensor-major and time-major) are computed so the features do not depend on the column order. Features are built from unscaled inputs and standardised internally.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.kernel_ridge import KernelRidge

class PhysFeatKRR(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):
    def __init__(self, alpha=1e-3, gamma_mult=1.0, eps=1e-3):
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.gamma_mult = gamma_mult
        self.eps = eps

    def _feat(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        n = X.shape[0]
        L = np.log(np.clip(np.abs(X), self.eps, None))
        feats = [X, L]
        if X.shape[1] == 80:
            layouts = [L.reshape(n, 4, 20), L.reshape(n, 20, 4).transpose(0, 2, 1)]
        else:
            layouts = []
        for A in layouts:
            T = A.shape[2]
            t = np.arange(T, dtype=float)
            tc = t - t.mean()
            slope = (A * tc).sum(2) / (tc ** 2).sum()
            h = T // 2
            tl = t[h:] - t[h:].mean()
            late = (A[:, :, h:] * tl).sum(2) / (tl ** 2).sum()
            dt = np.diff(A, axis=2).reshape(n, -1)
            dsp = np.diff(A, axis=1).reshape(n, -1)
            feats += [slope, late, np.diff(slope, axis=1), dt, dsp]
        return np.hstack(feats)

    def fit(self, X, y):
        F = self._feat(X)
        self.mu_ = F.mean(0)
        self.sd_ = F.std(0) + 1e-8
        Z = (F - self.mu_) / self.sd_
        g = self.gamma_mult / Z.shape[1]
        self.model_ = KernelRidge(alpha=self.alpha, kernel='rbf', gamma=g)
        self.model_.fit(Z, y)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        Z = (self._feat(X) - self.mu_) / self.sd_
        return self.model_.predict(Z)

def build_model(params, task, seed):
    kw = {k: params[k] for k in ('alpha', 'gamma_mult', 'eps') if k in params}
    return PhysFeatKRR(**kw)

data.advice:
No idea violates a constraint, leaks test data, or is certain to fail, so none are rejected. Guidance:

1. **Selection discipline.** Select models and hyperparameters only on the 750-sample val split, or on CV within train. Fit scalers and PCA on train only. Evaluate test once, at the end.

2. **Log and sqrt features.** Noisy temperatures near zero, especially at late times or near the Dirichlet ends, can be non-positive. Use a fixed clip such as log(max(u, eps)), with the same eps across ideas, or the log runs will produce NaN/inf or amplify noise. If the log runs underperform, compare them against the raw and sqrt variants.

3. **Target transform.** Conductivities are positive and act multiplicatively, so consider regressing log k and exponentiating back. Always compute rel_l2 on k in its original scale.

4. **Priorities.** Rank the MLPs (idea-010, 011, 013, 017), KRR (idea-002, 004) and the physics-feature KRR (idea-016) highest. Tree models (idea-006, 007, 008) rarely reach rel_l2 <= 0.05 on smooth inverse maps. Keep them as cheap references, but cap trees at about 200 and use n_jobs to stay within the 400 worker-second budget.

5. **Redundancy.** idea-002 and idea-004 overlap. Run both only if gamma and alpha are tuned on val, because a fixed gamma_mult can be badly off. Use idea-003 as the linear floor.

6. **Noise augmentation (idea-013).** Match noise_std to the actual measurement noise level after standardization.

7. **Reporting.** Report per-segment rel_l2. Conductivities in segments far from the sensors or near the boundaries may be poorly identifiable and dominate the error.

8. **Torch runtime.** Set torch threads to 1 per worker to avoid oversubscription across the 6 workers. Use early stopping on val loss.

author: ideator-classical
summary: Kernel ridge on sqrt features with wider bandwidth and lower alpha

data.title: Kernel ridge on sqrt features with wider bandwidth and lower alpha
data.hypothesis: sqrt features gave the best MLP result (0.0283), which suggests sqrt compresses dynamic range while keeping noise closer to homoscedastic than log, where noise at low temperatures gets amplified. Pairing sqrt with a wider kernel (gamma_mult=0.3) and less shrinkage (alpha=3e-4) should give a smoother interpolant that uses the 3000 samples better. Target: val rel_l2 below 0.028.

author: ideator-classical
summary: Log-feature kernel ridge with PCA-40 denoising and tuned bandwidth

data.title: Log-feature kernel ridge with PCA-40 denoising and tuned bandwidth
data.hypothesis: The 80 sensor-time features are highly correlated, and the trailing components mostly carry noise. Projecting onto 40 PCA components before the RBF kernel removes noise directions that inflate distances. Without that noise, a smaller alpha (5e-4) and a slightly narrower kernel (gamma_mult=0.7) become viable. This differs from the earlier PCA-KRR because it uses log features, a different PCA size and a re-tuned bandwidth. Target: val rel_l2 of about 0.026.

author: ideator-neural
summary: Tanh MLP on PCA-24 log features with wider layers and mild weight decay

data.title: Tanh MLP on PCA-24 log features with wider layers and mild weight decay
data.hypothesis: idea-011 (tanh, log, PCA-24) reached 0.0312. The smooth tanh map on decorrelated log-decay components looks capacity-limited rather than noise-limited. Widening to [512,512], raising weight_decay to 1e-4, using a slightly lower lr and running more epochs should cut approximation error without overfitting the 3000 samples. The batch size goes from 64 to 128 to keep cost within budget.

author: ideator-neural
summary: SiLU deep MLP on PCA-32 sqrt features (combine best activation/feature with PCA denoising)

data.title: SiLU deep MLP on PCA-32 sqrt features (combine best activation/feature with PCA denoising)
data.hypothesis: The best run so far, idea-017 (sqrt features, SiLU, [512,256,128], no PCA), scored 0.0283. idea-011 suggests that PCA denoising helps on noisy sensor data. Applying PCA-32 to the sqrt features removes high-variance noise directions while keeping the decay information from the four sensors. This should push val rel_l2 below 0.028, and the smaller input should also train faster.

author: ideator-domain
summary: Wider SiLU torch MLP on sqrt features with longer cosine schedule and light weight decay

data.title: Wider SiLU torch MLP on sqrt features with longer cosine schedule and light weight decay
data.hypothesis: idea-017 (0.0283) likely remains capacity/optimisation-limited at 150 epochs; the smooth sqrt-compressed decay signals map near-smoothly to k, so a wider [1024,512] SiLU net trained for 250 epochs with batch 64 and slightly lower lr should reduce bias while early stopping controls variance, pushing rel_l2 toward ~0.024.

author: ideator-domain
summary: SiLU torch MLP on log-temperatures (decay-rate linearisation) with mild dropout

data.title: SiLU torch MLP on log-temperatures (decay-rate linearisation) with mild dropout
data.hypothesis: Log features linearise exponential modal decay (log u ~ -lambda(k) t), which made log the best transform for KRR (0.0298); combining that physics-motivated transform with idea-017's deeper SiLU architecture plus small dropout (0.05) to regularise against sensor noise amplified by the log should match or beat the sqrt variant and provide a diverse ensemble candidate.

author: critic
summary: critic advice: All six ideas are aligned with the objective and use only simulated train/val data, so none are rejected. The current best (0.0283) already

data.advice: All six ideas are aligned with the objective and use only simulated train/val data, so none are rejected. The current best (0.0283) already meets the 0.05 target, so prioritise robustness and confirming results over chasing small gains. (1) Select only on val. Report val rel_l2 averaged over at least 2 seeds for the torch MLPs, because differences of about 0.001 between 0.028 and 0.031 are likely seed noise. (2) idea-022 (1024x512, batch 64, 250 epochs) is the most expensive. Watch per-worker wall time against the 400 s total budget and use early stopping on val loss. (3) idea-023 and idea-019 use log features. Confirm the existing log transform clips or offsets non-positive noisy temperatures (e.g. log(max(u, eps))), as earlier log runs presumably did. (4) For the KRR runs (018, 019), sweep alpha and gamma over a small grid on val rather than fixing single values, since KRR is cheap. (5) Consider predicting log k and checking that rel_l2 is computed on k in the original scale. (6) A cheap next step is a val-weighted ensemble of the best MLP and the best KRR, fit on train and weighted on val only, which often beats either model alone.
